title: AI in insurance: what are carriers, MGAs and TPAs using it for?
description: AI in insurance, ranked by payoff for carriers, MGAs and TPAs. Policy and claims analytics, the state AI rules, and what examiners now ask.
verdict: AI informs; people decide.[^1] Of 193 auto insurers in 2022, 96 used AI to inform adjusters; none to deny claims.[^2]
Start where reading piles up: submission intake for underwriters and complex claim files for adjusters.[^3][^4]
For managing general agents (MGAs), clean portfolio data is becoming a condition for capacity.[^5] MGA premium grew 12% in 2025.[^6]
Thirty jurisdictions use the National Association of Insurance Commissioners (NAIC) AI bulletin.[^7] A new supplement lists regulators' AI questions.[^45]
Keep a named person on every claim denial. Lawsuits claiming algorithms, not reviewers, drove health denials have partly survived dismissal.[^9][^10]

headings.ranked: Where does AI pay first in insurance?
headings.buy-or-build: Should you buy AI tools or build your own?

summary: AI in insurance reads and drafts for underwriters and adjusters, and scores prices, renewals and claims.[^3][^11][^57] People keep the decision: state regulators apply the same standards whatever tool you use.[^12][^8] Clean data and a real human check make or break it.[^13][^9]
humanRole: Underwriters keep accept, decline and price. New York expects each adverse decision to state the information used and its source.[^14][^15]
Adjusters keep every claim denial, at carriers and third-party administrators (TPAs) alike. In the regulators' auto survey, 9 of 193 insurers used AI for claim approvals and none for denials.[^2]
MGA underwriters keep the bind decision within their authority. Carriers' AI programs should cover AI from outside firms, so expect their questions.[^8]
At large agencies, a licensed person checks anything a client sees. Verify limits, deductibles, exclusions and endorsements against the policy forms.[^16]

Senior management and the board own the AI program, with a committee from underwriting, claims, compliance and legal.[^12][^8] The bulletin lists checking AI against expert review as one way to validate it.[^8]
Reviewers need the authority to reverse, change or escalate AI output, and their overrides should be logged. The NAIC's new AI supplement asks about both.[^46][^44]

ranked.name: Submission intake and triage (carriers and MGAs)
ranked.why: Underwriters spend up to 40% of their time on admin and other non-core work.[^3] Only 9% of underwriting leaders use AI to read and prepare submission data to a large extent; 68% expect to in three years.[^17]
ranked.payoff: Hours from submission received to quote, and the share of submissions quoted.

ranked.name: Claim file summaries for adjusters (carriers)
ranked.why: Claims is the top AI area for auto insurers, and the main use is informing adjusters.[^2][^18] Aviva, a large UK carrier, reports over £90m of claims savings[^65]; McKinsey says it assesses complex liability 23 days faster.[^4]
ranked.payoff: Adjuster minutes per file review, and days to final payment (40.7 on average for US home claims in 2026).[^19]

ranked.name: Claims analytics: severity, litigation and recovery (carriers and TPAs)
ranked.why: Sedgwick reports litigated general liability claims cost over 5.5 times others, and 47% had an attorney on day one.[^53] Attorney involvement in auto injury claims rose from 40% to nearly 50% by 2022.[^52]
ranked.payoff: Days from claim report to first adjuster contact on high-risk claims, and dollars recovered from at-fault parties (subrogation).

ranked.name: Pricing, renewal and loss-ratio analytics (carriers and MGAs)
ranked.why: In WTW's survey of property and casualty (P&C) insurers, analytics leaders spent about 6 cents less per premium dollar on claims and costs.[^64] That's a link, not proof; models can also flag the riskiest submissions for underwriters.[^64][^61]
ranked.payoff: Loss ratio (claims per premium dollar) by class, territory and agent, and retention of your best renewals.

ranked.name: AI inventory and examiner file (carriers)
ranked.why: Examiners can ask for your written AI program, model inventory, validation work and vendor contracts.[^8] Only 24% of insurance leaders are very confident they could pass an independent AI governance review within 90 days.[^20]
ranked.payoff: Days to produce the examiner file, and the share of AI uses inventoried.

ranked.name: Bordereaux and carrier reporting (MGAs)
ranked.why: AM Best says consistent, transparent portfolio data is becoming a condition for MGAs' access to capital.[^5] It also reports added scrutiny of MGAs as the market matures.[^21]
ranked.payoff: Days to close each bordereau (the premium and claims report to a carrier), and carrier data queries per month.

ranked.name: Fraud screening (carriers)
ranked.why: Fraud costs US consumers $308.6 billion a year, a coalition figure the NAIC cites.[^22] Among insurers the regulators surveyed, 58% in auto and 55% in home use, plan or explore AI for fraud detection.[^18]
ranked.payoff: Hit rate of referrals to your special investigations unit, checked by customer group.

ranked.name: Policy checking and coverage comparison (large agencies)
ranked.why: Coverage form analysis is the second most common AI use among independent agencies, at 43%.[^23] A qualified person still verifies limits, deductibles, exclusions and endorsements against the policy.[^16]
ranked.payoff: Minutes per policy check, and errors caught before the client sees the policy.

ownData.title: What are your peers hiring for?
ownData.intro: We counted US insurance job ads posted in the 30 days to 26 November 2026, by job title, in one job-ad database.[^24] An ad counts as mentioning AI if it names artificial intelligence, generative AI, ChatGPT, Copilot, AI tools, AI-powered or machine learning.[^24] AI shows up in modeling jobs far more than in the front-line jobs where the admin piles up.[^24][^3]

tables.title: What do policy and claims models predict, and what does the person decide?
tables.intro: Policy and portfolio analytics cover pricing, risk selection, renewals and loss-ratio drivers.[^57][^61] Claims analytics cover severity, litigation, fraud and recovery.[^11][^64] Ireland's central bank found insurers' AI mostly assisted, with none fully autonomous.[^66]

rows.name: Pricing
cells: Expected claim frequency and severity by rating factor, from a generalized linear model (GLM) or gradient boosting.[^57][^58][^59] No model won on both accuracy and fairness in a 2026 study.[^60]
The pricing actuary picks the final factors and files them; state rate reviewers check the model.[^57]

rows.name: Risk selection
cells: Predicted loss ratio for each submission, with extreme risks flagged for review.[^61]
The underwriter accepts, declines, prices or refers the risk.[^61]

rows.name: Renewal and lapse
cells: The chance a policy lapses, or renews at a loss.[^62][^63] Only 15% of underwriting leaders use AI heavily on renewals today.[^17]
The underwriter or account manager picks the action; a non-renewal stays a person's call.[^11]

rows.name: Loss-ratio drivers
cells: Which classes, territories or agents drive losses.[^61]
The head of underwriting sets appetite and agent terms.[^61]

rows.name: Claim severity
cells: Likely size of a new claim, from claim data, weather or report text.[^56][^68][^11]
The claims manager assigns the adjuster; the adjuster sets and owns the reserve.[^11]

rows.name: Litigation risk
cells: The chance an attorney gets involved.[^52][^53]
The adjuster makes early contact; defense counsel and the claims manager set strategy.[^53]

rows.name: Fraud flags
cells: A suspicion score for each claim.[^55][^22]
Special investigators decide whether to pursue a flag; in one field test, 51 of 100 held up.[^55] The adjuster decides to pay or deny.[^2]

rows.name: Subrogation
cells: Recovery potential, read from notes and police reports.[^54] Insurers recovered $51.6B through salvage and subrogation in 2021.[^54]
The recovery specialist decides whether and how to pursue.[^54]

rules.name: NAIC Model Bulletin on insurers' use of AI
rules.status: In force in 30 jurisdictions (NAIC map, 13 Nov 2026)
rules.what: You need a written AI program covering governance, risk controls and audit, scaled to the possible harm to consumers.[^12][^8] It covers vendor AI, and examiners can ask for your AI inventory, vendor contracts and testing.[^8] Recent adopters include Texas, South Carolina and North Dakota; check your state's own text.[^7]

rules.name: NAIC AI Risk Evaluation Supplement
rules.status: Adopted 17 Nov 2026; voluntary state use from 2027
rules.what: Regulators can use it to ask how many AI systems you run, how your AI program works, and about each high-risk model and its data.[^45][^46] It asks whether reviewers can reverse, modify or escalate AI output, and whether overrides are logged.[^46] Adopted after a 12-state pilot and offered to states for voluntary use,[^44][^67][^69] it creates no new legal duties on its own.[^45]

rules.name: Colorado SB21-169 and Regulation 10-1-1
rules.status: In force: life since Nov 2023; auto and health since 15 Oct 2025
rules.what: Life, private auto and health insurers need a board-overseen framework for outside consumer data and the models that use it.[^30][^31] Commercial-only carriers and MGAs writing only commercial lines are outside its scope today.[^30] Bias-testing reports are waived until the Division adopts testing rules for each line.[^32]

rules.name: Colorado SB26-189, automated decision-making law
rules.what: It re-enacts Colorado's AI Act as rules on automated decisions that affect consumers.[^51] Insurers covered by SB21-169 count as compliant for the practice of insurance.[^51] AI an insurer uses in hiring gets no such exemption.[^51]

rules.name: New York Department of Financial Services (DFS) Circular Letter No. 7
rules.what: New York insurers must show that AI and outside data in underwriting and pricing don't discriminate unfairly, with the board responsible.[^14] You stay responsible for vendor tools, so contracts should give audit rights.[^14] Adverse-decision notices should name the information used and its source.[^15]

rules.name: California Insurance Bulletin 2022-5
rules.what: California's own guidance on bias in AI and big data; the NAIC lists it in place of the model bulletin.[^7]

rules.name: NAIC third-party data and model vendor framework
rules.status: Draft re-exposed 16 Nov 2026; comments close end Dec 2026; adoption considered spring 2027
rules.what: It proposes a multi-state registry for vendors of property and casualty (P&C) pricing and underwriting data and models; registration is voluntary.[^33][^34][^47] Insurers would still own their own compliance.[^35][^47] Adoption will be considered in spring 2027.[^48]

rules.name: EU AI Act, Annex III point 5(c)
rules.what: AI used to assess risk and set prices for individuals in life and health insurance is high-risk.[^49][^50] The Digital Omnibus moved those duties to 2 Dec 2027.[^50] Motor, home, commercial, claims handling and fraud models are not in point 5(c).[^49]

watchOuts: Rubber-stamp review: a lawsuit alleges Cigna doctors denied over 300,000 payment requests at about 1.2 seconds each, and a court let it proceed.[^9][^36] Nothing is proven yet; still, log review time, sample decisions and show reviewers the evidence, not only the score.

Unequal outcomes: Black homeowners allege State Farm's claim-screening algorithms slowed and questioned their claims more; the claim survived dismissal in 2023.[^37] Test outcomes by group before and after go-live; Colorado and New York expect it for covered lines.[^30][^14]
Vendor AI treated as someone else's problem. The NAIC bulletin and New York keep you responsible for vendor models, so put audit rights and regulator cooperation in the contract.[^8][^14]

Controls you can't prove: 68% of insurance leaders say their AI controls exist, but the evidence is scattered across teams and tools.[^20] Keep one inventory entry and one evidence file per AI use, because examiners can ask for both.[^8]

Trusting a vendor's accuracy figure: score it on your own files against what your experts decided, a check the bulletin names.[^8] Data quality is insurers' second biggest AI barrier, named by 45%.[^13]

Pilots that never reach the desk: only 7% of carriers in a 2026 claims study report scalable AI success.[^38] Pilot one workflow on one team with one owner and one measure; few task-specific AI tools reach production.[^39]

faq.q: How is AI used in insurance?
faq.a: Insurers use AI mostly to read and draft for the people who decide.[^1][^11] In regulators' surveys, claims leads in auto, claims and underwriting run close in home, and underwriting leads in life.[^18] Conning names AI and data-driven underwriting among the drivers of MGA growth.[^6]

faq.q: What is a predictive model in insurance?
faq.a: A predictive model in insurance is a statistical or machine-learning model that estimates claim frequency, severity, lapse or fraud from past data.[^57][^63] State rate reviewers check both generalized linear models (GLMs) and gradient boosting machines in filings.[^57] Studies find gradient boosting often wins on claim frequency, but not always on severity.[^58][^59]

faq.q: What is insurance analytics, and how do insurers analyze claims data?
faq.a: Insurance analytics means using policy and claims data to find what drives losses, then acting on it.[^61][^11] For claims, models flag likely severity, attorney involvement, fraud and recovery chances so adjusters act early.[^11][^52][^54] Early action matters: represented auto injury claimants waited a median of about 440 days.[^52]

faq.q: Where should a carrier or MGA start with AI?
faq.a: A carrier or MGA should start with one reading-heavy workflow, such as submission intake or complex claim files.[^3][^17] Pick one with a clear before-and-after number. Add it to your AI inventory from day one, since examiners can ask for it.[^8]

faq.q: What is the best AI for insurance?
faq.a: No single AI is best for insurance: pick by job, such as submission intake, claim summaries, pricing or fraud.[^28][^25][^64] Check what your core system vendor already owns, then test any tool on your own files against your experts' calls.[^27][^8]

faq.q: What will the examiner ask about our AI?
faq.a: Examiners ask for your written AI program, your inventory of models and AI systems, and how you validate and monitor them.[^8] The NAIC's new AI Risk Evaluation Supplement, for voluntary state use from 2027, adds four exhibits: AI counts, your program, high-risk models and their data.[^45][^46][^69] For vendor AI, expect requests for your due diligence, contracts and audits.[^8][^12]

faq.q: Does the NAIC AI bulletin apply to MGAs?
faq.a: Not directly: the NAIC AI bulletin is addressed to insurers.[^12] Insurers must cover AI they rely on from outside firms, so carrier partners may ask an MGA about its AI.[^8] AM Best describes added scrutiny of MGAs as the market matures.[^21]

faq.q: Is AI going to replace insurance jobs?
faq.a: No: regulators find insurers' AI use mostly assisted, and underwriters and adjusters keep the decisions.[^66][^2] The NAIC says AI is more likely to support human workers than replace them.[^11] Only 16% of P&C insurers use AI to augment underwriters today; 60% plan to by 2028, WTW found.[^64]

faq.q: Which AI rules apply to insurers in my state?
faq.a: The NAIC AI bulletin applies in 30 jurisdictions (28 states, DC and Puerto Rico), per the NAIC map of 13 Nov 2026.[^7] California, Colorado and New York have their own guidance or rules.[^7] The map doesn't confirm each state kept every element, so read your state's own text.[^7]

faq.q: What does an AI platform for a carrier or MGA cost?
faq.a: One published list price runs from $1,667 a month for a 5-user MGA underwriting tool to $8,167 a month for its enterprise tier.[^70] Most carrier platforms, such as Hi Marley and Federato, publish no price, so budget from a scoped quote for one workflow.[^25][^26]

buyVsBuild.buy: Buy when the job is standard, such as submission intake or claims texting, and you have no data team.[^40] Most enterprise AI is now bought: 76% of use cases, up from 53% in 2024.[^40] MIT found vendor partnerships reached production about twice as often as internal builds.[^39][^41]
buyVsBuild.build: Build when your guidelines, appetite and loss history are your edge, or you must explain every step to an examiner.[^14][^8] A thin build on your own rules also avoids lock-in while the NAIC vendor registry is still a draft.[^33] A common middle path: buy the reading step, and keep the rules and the decision log yourself.

pickElse: Your core systems can't take the AI output: fix the integration first. Legacy integration is insurers' top barrier to scaling AI, named by 50%.[^13]
You already run Guidewire or Applied: check the AI they now own, such as hx and Cytora, before adding a separate tool.[^27][^28]
Your team only needs to write and summarise faster: an enterprise plan of ChatGPT, Claude or Microsoft 365 Copilot will do. Bring it into your AI program, which covers generative AI too.[^8]
Simple, high-volume claims: straight-through rules in your claims system may already do the job.[^42]

offer.heading: Which insurance workflow should you hand to AI first?
offer.body: Hand AI one reading-heavy workflow first: submission intake for underwriters, claim file summaries for adjusters, or bordereaux for MGAs. In 30 minutes we map that workflow. You leave knowing who signs off, the measure to track and what your examiner or carrier partner will ask.

reviews.notes: Retarget, 26 Nov 2026: the page read as a small-agency tool guide. Now ranks carrier, MGA and large-agency jobs, each with one measure. Cut agency tools priced by the month, the AI receptionist and the renewal-CRM tips: none leads a 40-500 person insurer to a decision. Added the examiner file as a job, since governance evidence is what COOs are asked for. Upgrade pass, 26 Nov 2026 (retarget to "AI in insurance"): new claims analytics and pricing analytics jobs each carry one measure. Swapped "first notice" jargon for plain "claim report" in the claims payoff.

Defined bordereaux in the ranked list. Pick-something-else now covers what an operations head actually hits: core-system integration, the AI already inside Guidewire or Applied, and simple claims that rules can handle. Tool table cut to four platforms with honest 'not published' prices so it fits a phone. Upgrade pass: new table of what each policy and claims model predicts and what the person decides, three columns so it fits a phone. Subrogation now explained on first use as recovery from at-fault parties.

MGA leaders get their own bottom-line bullet: capacity now follows clean portfolio data, with AM Best and Conning behind it. Added an FAQ on whether the NAIC bulletin reaches MGAs, worded carefully: it is addressed to insurers, who must cover outside AI. Offer now names carrier bordereaux and what a carrier partner will ask. Upgrade pass: the analytics payoff is put in margin terms, about 6 cents per premium dollar in WTW's survey, labelled as a link, not proof. Loss ratio now defined in the payoff line.

Head of underwriting or claims asks what the examiner will ask. Replaced a vendor's summary of the bulletin with Illinois's own copy of the text, which lists the examiner requests. Replaced a vendor-commissioned underwriter survey with Accenture's 430-executive survey. Claims payoff now has a public baseline: J.D. Power's 40.7 days to final payment. Upgrade pass: head of claims and head of underwriting get the NAIC AI Risk Evaluation Supplement, its override and escalation questions in "who signs off", the EU life and health listing and Colorado's new law. The examiner answer now says the supplement is voluntary for states from 2027, so it doesn't overstate.

Gets the answer in 10 seconds: title is his question and the bottom line is five short bullets. Forum quotes and AI-tool listicles are gone; every claim now rests on a regulator, a court record, a large survey or the vendor's own announcement. No case from a firm his size exists in the research, so none is claimed. Upgrade pass: title now leads with "AI in insurance" and still asks his question. "Regulators" in the bottom line now says state regulators. Aviva figures are labelled as a large UK carrier's, so he doesn't read them as his own scale.

answers.human-role: Your people keep every decision: underwriters accept, decline and price, MGA underwriters bind, and adjusters own every claim denial.[^14][^2][^8] Senior management and the board own the AI program, and a licensed person checks anything a client sees.[^12][^8][^16]
answers.ranked: AI pays first in submission intake for underwriters, then claim file summaries and claims analytics for adjusters.[^3][^17][^4][^53] For MGAs the early win is bordereaux and carrier reporting; for large agencies, policy checking.[^5][^23]
answers.own-data: Insurers ask for AI skills mostly in modeling jobs: about 1 in 4 actuary ads mention AI, against about 1 in 20 underwriter and claims ads.[^24] Agency sales and account ads mention AI least, about 1 in 40.[^24]
answers.table-1: Cytora, Federato, hyperexponential (hx) and Hi Marley are four AI platforms built for carriers and MGAs, all sold by quote or private offer with no published price.[^28][^25][^27][^26] Two now belong to bigger insurance software firms: Applied Systems bought Cytora, and Guidewire agreed to buy hx.[^28][^27]
answers.table-2: Auto insurers use or plan AI most for claims (80%), life insurers for underwriting (75%), and home insurers about equally for both (60% and 62%).[^18] Among health insurers, 54% use or plan AI for claim decisions.[^18]
answers.rules: The NAIC AI model bulletin applies in 30 jurisdictions, per the NAIC map of 13 Nov 2026. California, Colorado and New York have their own rules.[^7] A new NAIC supplement sets out what regulators can ask, and the EU AI Act covers life and health pricing from Dec 2027.[^45][^49][^50] The NAIC vendor framework is still a draft.[^47]
answers.what-goes-wrong: AI in insurance goes wrong when review becomes a rubber stamp, outcomes differ by group, or vendor models go unchecked.[^9][^37][^8] Scattered evidence of controls and pilots that never reach the desk are the other common failures.[^20][^38]
answers.buy-or-build: Buy the standard reading step, such as submission intake or claims texting, and build only where your guidelines, appetite and loss history are your edge.[^40][^14][^8] Bought tools reached production about twice as often as internal builds in MIT's study.[^39][^41]
answers.something-else: Pick something else when your core systems can't take AI output, your Guidewire or Applied stack already includes AI, or simple claims run fine on rules.[^13][^27][^28][^42] For plain writing and summaries, an enterprise plan of ChatGPT, Claude or Microsoft 365 Copilot will do, inside your AI program.[^8]
answers.table-3: Models predict a number, such as a price factor, lapse risk, claim size or fraud score.[^57][^11] A named person still decides: the actuary sets prices, the underwriter selects risks and the adjuster owns each claim.[^57][^61][^11]
